summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block for reporting burst and gap loss metrics. It can be used across a range of RTP applications to describe how packet loss is distributed.

eli5.summary: This is a report card telling whether lost audio or video packets vanished in clumps or one by one.

questions: reporting packet loss patterns in rtp
what is rtcp xr burst gap loss
what is a loss burst in rtp
how to measure packet loss burstiness
subtitle: An RTCP report block that says whether lost media packets vanish in clumps or one at a time.

tldr.problem: Two streams can lose the same number of packets yet sound or look very different, because losses that come in bursts hurt user experience more than scattered ones. Standard RTCP reports only a cumulative count of lost packets.
tldr.mechanism: A new RTCP Extended Report block, type 20, carries the number of loss bursts, the total time spent in bursts, the packets lost and expected inside bursts, and a sum of squared burst durations. A receiver can use these to work out the mean and variance of burst lengths.
tldr.outcome: Senders and monitoring systems get a statistical picture of how loss is distributed. The block is a Proposed Standard and applies to streams that do not use repair such as FEC or retransmission.

today: RFC 6958 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Report Burst and Gap Loss
sections.content:
RFC 6958 defines a new block type to augment the RTCP Extended Report (XR) framework of RFC 3611. The block reports the proportion of packets lost by the network and, in particular, the losses that happen during loss bursts. It also reports the number of bursts and enough extra data to calculate the mean and variance of the distribution of burst lengths.

The RFC says the block provides information on transient IP problems. The burstiness of packet loss affects user experience, may influence any sender strategies to mitigate the problem, and may also have diagnostic value. Burst/gap metrics are typically used in Cumulative reports, but they may also be used in Interval reports.

Some uses of the metrics depend on the metric "cumulative number of packets lost" from standard RTCP (RFC 3550). The metric belongs to the class of transport-related end system metrics defined in RFC 6792, and the block follows the guidelines of RFC 6390 and RFC 6792.
sections.eli5: A plain count of lost packets is like knowing only how many socks went missing. This report also tells you whether they all vanished in one laundry accident or one by one.

sections.title: Lost, Discarded, Bursts and Gaps
sections.content:
A packet is regarded as lost if it fails to arrive within an implementation-specific time window. A packet that arrives in that window but is too early or too late to be played out, or is thrown away because of duplication or redundancy, is discarded. Every packet is classified as received, discarded or lost.

RTCP XR views a stream as divided into bursts, periods when the loss rate is high enough to cause noticeable quality degradation (generally over 5 percent), and gaps, periods when lost packets are infrequent and quality is generally acceptable. This is consistent with RFC 3611.

To suit different jitter buffer algorithms, an implementation may use a method equivalent to the one in RFC 3611 to tell bursts from gaps. It should give the same result for burst packet loss, but may differ under time-varying jitter.

The metrics are for RTP applications that contain jitter buffers and do not use stream repair such as Forward Error Correction (RFC 5109) or retransmission (RFC 4588).
sections.eli5: A burst is a bad stretch where lots of packets go missing, like a patch of road full of potholes. A gap is a smooth stretch between the bad patches.

sections.title: The Burst/Gap Loss Metrics Block
sections.content:
The block is measured at the receiving end of the RTP stream. It begins with the block type BT=20, a two-bit Interval Metric flag I, a one-bit Loss and Discard Combination flag C, five reserved bits and a Block Length of 5. Next comes the SSRC of the source, and then the metric fields: Threshold, Sum of Burst Durations (ms), Packets Lost in Bursts, Total Packets Expected in Bursts, Number of Bursts, and Sum of Squares of Burst Durations (ms-squared).

The Threshold is equivalent to Gmin in RFC 3611: the number of successive packets that must be received before and after a lost packet for that packet to count as part of a gap.

The I flag says what period the numbers cover: 10 for the most recent interval, 11 for a cumulative period. Senders MUST NOT use 00 or 01, and a receiver MUST discard a block that has either. The C flag is set to 1 when the loss/discard report is combined with this report in the same compound RTCP packet. Reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt. A block whose length is not 5 MUST be discarded.

Each block refers by SSRC to a Measurement Information Block (RFC 6776) that describes the measurement period. Senders MUST send the two in the same compound RTCP packet, and a receiver MUST discard this block if the measurement period did not arrive in the same compound packet.
sections.eli5: The block is a small form with boxes to fill in: how many bad patches there were, how long they lasted in total, and how many packets went missing inside them.

sections.title: Field Sizes and Special Values
sections.content:
The duration, packet and burst counts are unsigned values. Sum of Burst Durations, Packets Lost in Bursts and Total Packets Expected in Bursts are 24 bits each; Number of Bursts is 16 bits; Sum of Squares of Burst Durations is 36 bits; Threshold is 8 bits.

Each metric has two reserved values. If the measurement is larger than the maximum minus 2, the sender MUST report the maximum minus 1 (for the 24-bit fields, 0xFFFFFE) to flag an over-range value. If the measurement is unavailable, it MUST report the all-ones value (0xFFFFFF for 24-bit fields, 0xFFFF for the burst count, 0xFFFFFFFFF for the sum of squares).

Total Packets Expected in Bursts is the sum of received packets and lost packets during the bursts.
sections.eli5: If a number is too big for its box, the sender writes a special "too big" code. If it could not measure at all, it writes a different special code that means "don't know".

sections.title: Derived Metrics and VoIP Use
sections.content:
The reported values are intended for use with the Measurement Information Block and with the standard RTCP "cumulative number of packets lost". From them one can derive the burst loss rate, the gap loss rate, and the mean and variance of burst duration, as detailed in the summary statistics work cited by the RFC.

For Voice-over-IP, a call is viewed as bursts, where quality is noticeably degraded (generally over 5 percent loss), and gaps, where it is generally acceptable. If Voice Activity Detection is used, burst and gap durations are determined as if silence packets had been sent, so a period of silence longer than Gmin packets ends a burst. The recommended Gmin value from RFC 3611 gives a burst whose quality degradation is similar to a typical Pulse Code Modulation Severely Errored Second.
sections.eli5: With these numbers a monitor can work out averages, such as how long a typical bad patch lasted. For phone calls, silence counts as if quiet packets had been sent, so a quiet pause can end a bad patch.

sections.title: SDP Signaling and IANA
sections.content:
RFC 3611 defines how the Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566) signals use of XR blocks, though XR blocks MAY be used without prior signaling. This RFC extends the rtcp-xr attribute with a new xr-format value, burst-gap-loss. Offer/answer usage follows the rules for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters in RFC 3611.

IANA assigns block type value 20 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry to the Burst/Gap Loss Metrics Block, and registers the burst-gap-loss parameter in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry.
sections.eli5: Two programs can agree ahead of time that they will use this report by naming it in their setup message. The report also gets its own official number, 20.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The block gives no per-packet statistics, so the confidentiality risk noted in RFC 3611 does not apply. However, the gaps it indicates could be used to detect the timing of other events on the path. For example, a competing multimedia stream might cause a loss burst for its duration, letting the receiver of the block know when that stream was active.

The RFC says this is not a significant threat because only the timing of the loss is leaked, not the cause. It believes the block introduces no other new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3611.
sections.eli5: Someone reading the reports could guess when something else was busy on the network, but not what it was, so the RFC says the risk is small.

items.label: Interval
items.desc: Value applies to the most recent interval between successive reports.

items.label: Cumulative
items.desc: Value applies to the accumulation period of cumulative measurements.

items.label: Sampled
items.desc: Not allowed for this block; receivers MUST discard it.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Reserved for future use; senders MUST NOT use it.
